Or was it simply the result of Christian theological influence transmitted through the man said to have been called Sansawayh, or Sawsan as Ibn Qutayba calls him in al-Maʿārif, and who is also mentioned in Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl? He was said to have been a Christian, then to have converted to Islam, then returned to Christianity, and to have influenced Maʿbad al-Juhanī.

If “philosophical necessity” alone explains the doctrine, why did this necessity appear at this particular moment rather than before or after it?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Why did this particular side of the attempt to reconcile Qurʾānic passages—the side supporting human freedom—appeal to so many people in Iraq and the Hijaz, and later in Damascus?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
By contrast, the doctrine of compulsion first appeared through Jahm ibn Ṣafwān in Tirmidh, in the region of Marw in Persia, and through al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Najjār in Rayy, also in Persia.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Why, then, did Qadarite doctrine flourish in Arab regions closely connected, directly or indirectly, to the political struggle between the Umayyad party and the various political forces opposed to it, while the doctrine of compulsion first grew in a different, Persian environment?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

And how could the limited personal influence of one individual—Maʿbad al-Juhanī’s supposed influence from Sansawayh—turn into a broad intellectual movement that rapidly spread among people from many social groups outside the ruling class, including religious scholars in a conservative region such as the Hijaz?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
If that personal influence really occurred, how could it grow into such a wide and powerful intellectual phenomenon unless another factor—social or political—helped produce that transformation?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Early historians and later researchers give us historical material that can shed a great deal of light on all these questions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This material allows us to reach a more realistic understanding of the problem than the one usually found in the studies available to us.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

We call these “historical materials” because the historians and researchers who recorded them generally treated them simply as pieces of information. They did not use them to build a broader interpretation beyond the historical narrative itself.

Yet they usually pass over them without trying to use them to uncover the social and political roots of the problem of human freedom and divine decree.

Maʿbad al-Juhanī and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī raised the question in Iraq. Ghaylān al-Dimashqī and ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ raised it in Damascus. From there, the question helped set Arab thought as a whole moving further along the road toward philosophical thinking.

They were the rulers of the Muslims themselves: the Umayyad rulers. At that time, Muslims had no other kings.

What exactly were they complaining about?

The historical evidence is perfectly clear. It answers the question without any need for interpretation.

“These kings shed Muslim blood and take Muslim wealth.”

And they did not stop there.

They justified these acts of oppression by saying that they “happen by God’s decree.”

In other words, they shed blood and seized property, then attributed their actions to God—to God’s decree and destiny, to a divine compulsion imposed on Muslims from which there was no escape.

Here we can clearly see that the question of divine decree had acquired a direct political and social meaning.
